findings.summary: The album era (mid-1960s to mid-2000s) was a period when the album, rather than the single, dominated popular music consumption. It was driven primarily by three physical formats: the 33⅓ rpm LP record, the cassette tape, and the compact disc. Rock musicians from the US and UK were often at the forefront. The era began in earnest when The Beatles released ambitious LPs like Rubber Soul in 1965, which helped normalize the album as an artistically unified work. Throughout its duration, the industry shifted toward album-oriented marketing, including lead singles, music videos, and concert tours. While rock remained central, women, Black musicians, and the hip hop genre gained recognition and developed their own album-based standards. The era peaked in 1999 at $15 billion in revenue, driven by CD sales. Its decline began with file-sharing networks like Napster in the early 2000s, followed by music downloading and streaming services, which shifted focus toward singles and effectively ended the album era.

mechanisms.title: Format-driven market shift
mechanisms.explanation: The transition from 78 rpm singles to LPs, then cassettes and CDs, expanded capacity and durability, enabling the album to become the dominant commercial unit. Each format change prompted industry responses, such as price increases for CDs and marketing rollouts centered on new releases.

mechanisms.title: Artist-driven conceptual unification
mechanisms.explanation: The emergence of the concept album, notably propelled by The Beatles' Rubber Soul, transformed the album from a collection of songs into a narrative work with a single theme. This artistic shift was later reinforced by marketing strategies that tied album releases to lead singles, music videos, and supporting tours.

unknowns: The extent to which non-rock genres fully adopted album-oriented consumption during the era
The specific economic impact of marketing rollouts on overall industry revenue beyond CD sales
The role of regional differences in the duration and intensity of the album era
The precise mechanisms by which streaming services replaced album-focused consumption patterns
